#### Defaults

The defaults are the prompts saved in this application's own repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, named as a project's are. They are the source of truth for the defaults, and are baked into the application when it is built, so a build always ships with whatever those files say, and changing them changes the defaults the next build has. A build can't be made without them.
The system template's default says what the project is, where its code is and where its spec is, each on a paragraph of its own, so the one a run can't see goes, that each prompt starts with a <task-instructions> block saying what that prompt is for and what it may change, and then SPEC_READING on a paragraph of its own. It holds no fluency.
The spec-reading prompt's default says:
Read the spec from its compiled reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

Never read the .pi source under ${SPEC_LOCATION} to learn what the spec says; that is only where edits to the spec go.

Before executing anything, read the spec it touches. Links to ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/... in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one you need before changing anything it covers. Don't re-read something you've already read.
The Spec and Chain defaults have, after what the mode is for, on a paragraph of its own:
Before creating or editing any .pi file, read ${PITON_FLUENCY_FILE} once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.
and then, on another:
Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, not by reading the source again.
The Code, Chain, and Spec defaults then end with, on a paragraph of its own:
Before changing anything, write the constraints this task must meet to ${UNDERSTANDING_FILE}, and keep it current as you read more of the spec. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.
The Ask default says what a question is for, and that it changes nothing, and, on a paragraph of its own, that SPEC_LOCATION is the spec's Piton source, there for `piton slice`, which the question reads the spec through, read only and never edited, and never read directly to learn what the spec says. Since a question can see the spec location, that paragraph is always sent with it. The Spec and Chain defaults never name the code location, and the Code default names the spec location only on a paragraph of its own, which goes where the run can't see it.
The defaults are only where a project starts, and what resetting a prompt puts back. A project whose prompts were saved before a default changed keeps them as they are.

content.text:
The real `code.md` isn't visible from here. It lives in the app's `.suspense/system-prompts/`, and this run can't see that folder. So below is the Code prompt as the spec defines it, with two gaps filled in. Only the last paragraph is fixed word for word by the spec, in ModeSystemPromptsScope › Defaults. For the rest, the spec says what each part must do but not its words. I matched the wording of the Spec and Chain blocks you've been sending me. I didn't change the spec.

```
We're working on the code, located in ${CODE_LOCATION}. Change the code so it does what the prompt asks, as the spec describes it.

The spec's Piton source is in ${SPEC_LOCATION}. Don't change it, and don't read it to learn what the spec says: read the compiled reference instead, as above. If the prompt asks for something the spec doesn't describe, or describes differently, say so in your reply rather than working around it.

Before changing anything, write the constraints this task must meet to ${UNDERSTANDING_FILE}, and keep it current as you read more of the spec. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.
```

How it lines up with the spec:
- **First paragraph:** says what the mode is for. That part is required, but its wording is up to us.
- **Second paragraph:** the spec location is named only in a paragraph of its own. That paragraph is dropped whenever a run can't see the spec location, and kept for a Code task on the host. It agrees with the host rules: a Code task may not edit the spec location and is told not to read it. The last sentence, about saying so when the spec and the prompt disagree, is my addition.
- **Third paragraph:** the understanding-file paragraph, word for word as the spec requires.
- **Nothing else:** there's no fluency pointer, since Code instructions must never mention it. "Read the compiled reference" is covered by `SPEC_READING`, which the system template already sends. The whole thing goes at the top of the message in a `<task-instructions>` block.

I can write this into the spec as the exact Code default, or you can paste it into Settings → System prompts → Code for this project.
